intro: Los Cabos is famous for its desert sunshine, and that is exactly why so many travelers come. But long hours on the beach, a fishing charter under a clear sky, a round of golf or a pool party with a few margaritas can drain your body of fluid faster than you expect — even outside the hottest summer months.

Dehydration and heat exhaustion are common, usually manageable and often preventable. Heat stroke, on the other hand, is a medical emergency. This guide explains how to spot the difference, what to do in the first few minutes, when to call 911, and how to have an English-speaking doctor come to your hotel, villa or yacht in Cabo San Lucas, the Tourist Corridor or San José del Cabo.

sections.h2: Why travelers get dehydrated in Cabo
p: Visitors often arrive from cooler, more humid places and spend their first days doing far more in the sun than they would at home. Common reasons we see:
list: Strong sun and dry desert air. Sweat evaporates quickly, so you may not notice how much fluid you are losing.
Alcohol in the heat. Drinks by the pool or on a boat add to fluid loss and make it harder to notice early warning signs.
Active days: hiking, golf, surfing, snorkeling, ATV tours and long walks around town.
Travel day fatigue: early flights, little sleep and skipped meals.
Stomach upsets: vomiting or diarrhea can dehydrate you quickly, especially in the heat.
Sunburn, which also draws fluid to the skin and can make you feel unwell.

sections.h2: Signs of dehydration and heat exhaustion
p: These two often go together. Watch for them in yourself and in the people you are traveling with, especially children and older relatives:

list: Strong thirst and a dry mouth or lips
Dark yellow urine, or urinating much less than usual
Headache and tiredness
Dizziness or lightheadedness when you stand up
In children: fewer wet diapers, no tears when crying, unusual sleepiness
Heavy sweating with cool, pale or clammy skin
Weakness, fatigue and muscle cramps
Headache, nausea or vomiting
Fast, weak pulse
Dizziness or a brief fainting spell
Body temperature that may be normal or slightly raised

p_after: Heat exhaustion is your body's warning that it is struggling to cool down. Acting quickly usually stops it from getting worse.

p: Heat stroke happens when the body can no longer control its temperature. It can develop from heat exhaustion or come on suddenly, and it needs emergency care. Signs include:
list: A very high body temperature, around 103°F (39.4°C) or higher
Confusion, slurred speech, strange behavior or agitation
Hot, red skin that may be dry or damp
A strong, rapid pulse
Seizures, fainting or loss of consciousness
p_after: Call 911 right away if you suspect heat stroke. While you wait, move the person to the shade or an air-conditioned room, loosen tight clothing and cool them with cool water, wet towels or a fan. Do not give fluids to anyone who is confused, very drowsy or unconscious.

sections.h2: What to do in the first few minutes
p: For mild dehydration or early heat exhaustion, these general first-aid steps often help:
list: Get out of the sun into shade or an air-conditioned room.
Lie down and rest, with your legs slightly raised if you feel faint.
Cool down: loosen clothing, use cool damp towels on the neck and armpits, take a cool (not ice-cold) shower or sit in front of a fan.
Sip fluids slowly: bottled or purified water, or an electrolyte drink. Small, frequent sips are easier to keep down than gulping.
Skip alcohol and heavy caffeine for the rest of the day.
Check again in 30 to 60 minutes. If you are not clearly improving, get medical help.
p_after: Ask a doctor or pharmacist before taking any medicine, especially for children, during pregnancy, or if you take other medication or have health conditions such as heart or kidney disease. Some common medications can make it harder for the body to handle heat.

p: Arrange a doctor visit the same day if:
list: Symptoms do not improve within about an hour of resting, cooling and drinking
You cannot keep fluids down because of vomiting
You have diarrhea along with signs of dehydration
You fainted, even briefly, or feel dizzy every time you stand
The person affected is a baby or young child, an adult over 65, someone pregnant, or someone with diabetes, heart, kidney or lung disease
You are worried about flying home while you still feel weak
p_after: Call 911 for any signs of heat stroke, confusion, a seizure, chest pain, trouble breathing, or if someone cannot be woken up.

sections.h2: How to prevent heat problems on your trip
list: Drink water steadily through the day — do not wait until you are thirsty.
Alternate every alcoholic drink with a glass of water.
Plan hikes, golf and long walks for early morning or late afternoon.
Wear a hat, sunglasses and light, loose clothing, and reapply sunscreen often.
Take shade breaks on boats and beaches, and bring extra water on excursions.
Eat regular meals; salty snacks and fruit help replace what you sweat out.
Give yourself a lighter first day after a long travel day.
Keep a close eye on kids and older family members, who may not say they feel unwell.

faq.q: What is the difference between heat exhaustion and heat stroke?
faq.a: Heat exhaustion usually causes heavy sweating, weakness, dizziness, nausea and cool, clammy skin, and often improves with rest, cooling and fluids. Heat stroke is an emergency: the body temperature rises very high and the person may become confused, faint or have a seizure. Call 911 right away for suspected heat stroke.

faq.q: Is it hot in Cabo in the winter?
faq.a: Winter days in Los Cabos are usually warm and sunny rather than extremely hot, but the strong sun, dry air, activity and alcohol can still lead to dehydration. Drinking water regularly and taking shade breaks matters year-round.

faq.q: When should I go to the hospital for heat illness?
faq.a: Call 911 for confusion, a very high temperature, fainting that does not quickly resolve, a seizure, chest pain, trouble breathing, or if someone cannot be woken up. These can be signs of heat stroke or another serious problem.
